clinicalPearls: The aorta is uniquely prone to aneurysm and rupture because, per Laplace's law, wall tension rises with the product of pressure and radius, so dilation begets further dilation; normal adult diameters are roughly 3.5 cm at origin/ascending, 2.5 cm in descending thoracic, and 1.8-2.0 cm in the abdomen.

True aneurysms involve all three wall layers; pseudoaneurysms have disrupted intima and media, with the dilated segment contained only by adventitia (and sometimes perivascular clot). Aneurysms are described as fusiform (whole circumference) or saccular (focal outpouching).

A contemporary threshold for an aneurysm of the aortic root/ascending aorta is diameter >=4.5 cm, while 4.0-4.4 cm is termed aortic dilation; descending thoracic and abdominal aneurysms are defined when dilated >=50% beyond the adjacent normal segment.

Medial degeneration (loss of medial smooth muscle and breakdown of collagen/elastin with mucoid/proteoglycan clefts) preferentially affects the proximal aorta and underlies ascending aneurysms in Marfan, Loeys-Dietz, vascular Ehlers-Danlos, bicuspid aortic valve, Turner, and familial thoracic aortic aneurysm syndromes; atherosclerosis is the dominant cause of descending thoracic and abdominal aneurysms.

Thoracic aortic aneurysms grow on average about 0.1-0.2 cm/year and are usually asymptomatic; symptoms (chest pain, dyspnea, cough, hoarseness, dysphagia) arise from compression/erosion, and ascending dilation can cause aortic regurgitation and heart failure.

Aortic dissection classically presents with sudden, severe, tearing chest or interscapular pain with diaphoresis that migrates as the dissection propagates; complications include syncope, pulse deficits, acute aortic regurgitation, pulmonary edema, and end-organ ischemia (stroke, paraplegia, bowel/renal/myocardial ischemia).

Stanford type A dissection involves the ascending aorta; type B is limited to arch and/or descending aorta. The type A/B scheme is more practical for management than the DeBakey I/II/III classification because DeBakey I and II are managed similarly.

Acute aortic regurgitation complicates more than 50% of proximal (type A) dissections, producing bounding pulses, wide pulse pressure, and a diastolic murmur along the right sternal border; retrograde type A dissection can cause hemopericardium and tamponade.

Intramural hematoma (rupture of the vasa vasorum, no intimal flap) and penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer are dissection variants, mostly in the descending thoracic aorta, and either can progress to dissection, false aneurysm, or rupture.

Abdominal aortic aneurysms are more common in men, increase with age, and at least 90% of those >4.0 cm are atherosclerotic and infrarenal; they are usually silent and found as a pulsatile, expansile, nontender mass, while new aneurysmal pain is a harbinger of impending rupture.

An ECG without ischemic changes helps distinguish aortic dissection from myocardial infarction in a patient with chest pain; rarely the dissection involves a coronary ostium (usually right) and causes acute MI.

Acute occlusion of the distal abdominal aorta is an emergency threatening limb viability, usually from a cardiac-origin saddle embolus, presenting with rest pain, coolness, pallor, and bilaterally absent distal pulses.

Aortic occlusive disease from atherosclerosis is typically infrarenal and, when extending to the iliacs, can cause Leriche syndrome (buttock/thigh/calf claudication with impotence in men) and absent femoral pulses with an abdominal bruit.
harrison.pathophysiology: The aortic wall comprises a thin endothelial intima, a thick smooth muscle/elastin/collagen tunica media, and a connective-tissue adventitia carrying the vasa vasorum. Continuous high pulsatile pressure and shear stress predispose it to injury. Aneurysms result from degradation or abnormal production of structural elastin and collagen; degenerative (most common, atherosclerosis-associated) aneurysms involve inflammation, oxidative stress, proteolysis (B/T lymphocytes, macrophages, cytokines, matrix metalloproteinases) and biomechanical stress, with histology showing elastin/collagen destruction, reduced smooth muscle, neovascularization, and inflammation. Heritable aneurysms reflect medial degeneration: fibrillin-1 deficiency (FBN1 mutation in Marfan) impairs elastic-fiber microfibrils and increases TGF-beta signaling, while Loeys-Dietz arises from mutations in TGF-beta isoforms/receptors and SMAD3; vascular Ehlers-Danlos involves COL3A1 (type III procollagen) mutations. Dissection begins with an intimal tear (often the right lateral ascending aorta or just below the ligamentum arteriosum) or medial hemorrhage, with pulsatile flow splitting the elastic lamellae to create a false lumen that usually propagates distally. Aortitis is inflammation of the wall (vasculitic, rheumatic, or infective) that may produce aneurysmal dilation, aortic regurgitation, or branch occlusion.
additionalDifferentials: Acute mesenteric ischemia (when abdominal pain predominates)
Renal colic or other causes of flank/back pain
infectionMimics: Syphilitic aortitis (late luetic infection, typically proximal ascending aorta)
Tuberculous aortic aneurysm (extension from hilar nodes/contiguous abscess)
Mycotic aneurysm from Staphylococcus, Streptococcus, Salmonella, or fungi seeding atherosclerotic plaque
nonInfectiousMimics: Giant cell arteritis with aortic involvement
Rheumatic aortitis (rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis and other HLA-B27 spondyloarthropathies, relapsing polychondritis, IBD-associated)
Connective-tissue aortopathies (Marfan, Loeys-Dietz, vascular Ehlers-Danlos) and fibromuscular dysplasia
additionalInvestigations: Chest x-ray (widened mediastinum, displaced/compressed trachea or left main bronchus; left pleural effusion in dissection)
Contrast-enhanced CT angiography (rapid, most commonly used for dissection; sensitivity/specificity >90%)
MRI/MR angiography (intimal flap, extent, branch involvement, intramural hematoma, penetrating ulcer)
Transthoracic echocardiography (overall sensitivity 60-85%; >80% for proximal ascending dissection)
Transesophageal echocardiography (about 98% sensitivity, ~90% specificity for ascending and descending dissection; less useful for the arch)
Abdominal ultrasound (sizing and surveillance of AAA, detection of mural thrombus; screening tool)
Blood cultures (frequently positive in mycotic aneurysm and infective aortitis)
ESR and C-reactive protein (elevated in active Takayasu and other aortitides)
Genetic testing in ascending thoracic aortic disease with features of Marfan/Loeys-Dietz/vascular Ehlers-Danlos or presentation under age 60
redFlags: Sudden severe tearing/migrating chest or interscapular pain with diaphoresis (acute dissection)
Acute hypotension or shock suggesting rupture or tamponade
New aortic regurgitation murmur, pulse deficits, or blood-pressure differential between limbs
Neurologic deficits (hemiplegia, paraplegia) indicating carotid or spinal cord ischemia
New or worsening aneurysmal pain (back, flank, scrotum) as a harbinger of AAA rupture
Acute limb ischemia with bilaterally absent distal pulses (acute aortic occlusion)
Fever, sepsis, and aortic/back pain with positive blood cultures (mycotic aneurysm/infective aortitis)
harrison.prognosis: Rupture risk rises with aneurysm size and symptoms: thoracic aneurysms carry roughly 2-3%/year rupture risk below 4.0 cm rising to about 7%/year above 6 cm; for abdominal aneurysms the 5-year rupture risk is about 1-2% under 5 cm versus 20-40% above 5 cm. Marfan and certain Loeys-Dietz/nonsyndromic familial aortopathies dissect at smaller diameters and expand faster. Elective AAA surgery with careful evaluation carries about 1-2% operative mortality, whereas emergent repair after rupture carries roughly 45-50% mortality. For dissection, in-hospital mortality is about 15-25% after type A surgery and around 12% for medically managed type B; with careful follow-up the 10-year survival after treated dissection is approximately 60%, though Marfan patients remain at high risk for post-dissection complications.
pitfalls: A left pleural effusion in dissection is usually serosanguineous and reactive, NOT necessarily a sign of rupture unless accompanied by hypotension and falling hematocrit.
About 25% of abdominal aortic aneurysms are not calcified and cannot be seen on plain x-ray, so a normal radiograph does not exclude an AAA.
Mural thrombus can reduce the luminal diameter, so contrast aortography may underestimate true aneurysm size.
Isolated direct vasodilators such as hydralazine are contraindicated in acute dissection because they raise hydraulic shear and heart rate and can propagate the dissection.
Transthoracic and even transesophageal echocardiography are relatively poor at imaging the aortic arch, a potential blind spot for dissection.
Serum IgG4 levels may be elevated but are not diagnostic of IgG4-related aortitis.
With adequate collateral flow, complete abdominal aortic occlusion can occur without ischemic symptoms, masking the severity of occlusive disease.
Genetic/heritable aortopathies warrant lower size thresholds for intervention; applying standard atherosclerotic thresholds risks under-treatment.
harrison.severityClassification: Aortic dissection: Stanford type A (involves ascending aorta, proximal) vs type B (arch and/or descending only, distal); DeBakey type I (ascending with propagation to arch/descending/abdominal), type II (limited to ascending), type III (descending with distal propagation). Type A/B is preferred for management decisions. Acute aortic syndromes encompass aortic rupture, dissection, intramural hematoma, and penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer.
management: Aggressive blood pressure control and reduction of aortic wall stress with beta-blockers, adding angiotensin receptor blockers particularly in Marfan syndrome, alongside statins and smoking cessation
Serial surveillance imaging of aneurysm diameter by echocardiography, CT or MRI at intervals guided by size and aetiology
Elective open surgical or endovascular repair once an aneurysm reaches its size threshold, grows rapidly or becomes symptomatic

Emergency management of acute dissection with intravenous beta-blockade and vasodilators to reduce heart rate and blood pressure, urgent surgery for ascending (type A) dissection and medical therapy for uncomplicated descending (type B) dissection
Emergency repair for rupture or impending rupture
Genetic counselling and family screening for heritable disease such as Marfan, Loeys-Dietz and vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndromes, bicuspid aortic valve and familial thoracic aortic aneurysm
Care coordinated by a multidisciplinary aortic team, with advice to avoid heavy isometric exertion while an aneurysm is present
